strengths: Addresses a focused and practically important problem: text-guided color editing with preservation of structure, materials, reflections, and non-edited regions in modern MM-DiT diffusion models.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and reasonably well motivated by the roles of different attention/value components: vision-to-vision attention for structure preservation, vision-to-text for mask extraction, vision values for non-edit-region preservation, and text-to-vision for attribute re-weighting.

Empirical coverage is broad: SD3 and FLUX.1-dev image editing, CogVideoX video editing, instruction-based editing models, real-image examples, ablations, commercial-model comparisons, and a user study.
Quantitative results consistently show strong gains in structural/background preservation metrics over training-free baselines, with relatively little loss in prompt/edit alignment.
The ablation study supports the utility of the two main components, and the paper provides useful implementation details for adapting several baselines to MM-DiT backbones.
The method appears practically useful: it does not require model training, can be applied across layers/timesteps, and extends naturally to video and instruction-editing settings.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The core idea is a targeted adaptation of prior attention-control and token-copying strategies to MM-DiT, and the paper could better distinguish what is fundamentally new from recombinations of Prompt-to-Prompt, MasaCtrl/DiTCtrl-style attention control, and value-token preservation.

The strongest claims about physical consistency, material preservation, reflections/refractions, and light-matter interaction are not rigorously evaluated. Canny/gradient SSIM, background PSNR/SSIM, CLIP, and GPT-4o-based VIEScore are useful proxies but do not directly validate physical correctness or disentangle albedo from illumination/material changes.

The main benchmark setting is noise-to-image rather than true editing of arbitrary real inputs, which weakens the practical editing claim. Real-image experiments are comparatively limited and depend on inversion quality, acknowledged as a limitation.

ColorCtrl-Bench is generated by an LLM, and the paper provides limited evidence about dataset quality, diversity, ambiguity, leakage, or annotation validation. The generated benchmark may overrepresent simple object-color substitutions and underrepresent difficult real editing cases.

Several baselines are reimplemented or retuned by the authors because official support is missing. Although details are provided, this leaves uncertainty about whether all baselines are operating at their best, especially given the sensitivity of these methods to layer/timestep choices.

The user study is small and somewhat oddly reported: all non-commercial training-free baselines receive 0% preference, which raises questions about comparison setup, case selection, and whether the study included sufficiently competitive or balanced outputs.

Commercial-model comparisons are interesting but not entirely controlled: closed models may optimize different objectives, and the paper emphasizes consistency while often accepting lower edit-success scores than GPT-4o/FLUX Kontext on some semantic metrics.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time because code is only promised upon acceptance. For a method depending on model-specific attention internals and baseline retuning, public code is particularly important.

Attribute re-weighting is demonstrated mostly qualitatively and only for the proposed method; there is no systematic evaluation of monotonicity, controllability, failure modes, or comparison to alternative token-scaling strategies.

The writing occasionally overstates conclusions, e.g. claims of preserving material properties and satisfying rendering constraints are stronger than the evidence supports. Some figures are dense and hard to inspect without zooming.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and well-scoped problem: training-free color editing with preservation of structure, background, and light-matter interactions.
The proposed attention/value-token interventions are simple and appear easy to plug into several MM-DiT backbones.
The paper includes comparisons across SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX, instruction-based editing models, commercial systems, ablations, real-image examples, and a small user study.
weaknesses: The core method appears quite incremental relative to Prompt-to-Prompt-style attention control, PnP/value-token replacement, and DiTCtrl; the paper does not clearly establish a substantial technical advance beyond choosing different MM-DiT attention blocks/quadrants for color editing.

The main benchmark setting is mostly noise-to-image rather than true editing of given images, which weakens the central claim of image/video editing and makes preservation easier than in realistic inversion-based workflows.

Several claims are too strong for the evidence, especially “physical consistency,” preservation of albedo/material/illumination, and “film industry-level” editing. The rendering formulation is largely conceptual and not actually estimated or validated.

The evaluation is potentially biased toward the proposed method: many baselines are reimplemented and manually tuned by the authors, some poor baseline settings are justified post hoc, and key comparisons depend on source images generated under the same setup as the proposed method.

ColorCtrl-Bench is generated by GPT with limited validation, and the prompt used for generation is included, but there is little evidence that the benchmark is diverse, unambiguous, or free of leakage/selection bias.

Metrics are not fully convincing. Canny/SSIM and background preservation mainly reward copying structure, CLIP is acknowledged as unreliable, and GPT-4o/VIEScore evaluation in the appendix introduces another opaque evaluator while GPT-4o is also a compared model.

The commercial-model comparison is not fully fair or diagnostic: these systems may optimize different editing objectives, and the paper often dismisses their higher semantic scores as “oversaturation” based on selective qualitative arguments.

The user study is underdescribed and somewhat implausible: all non-commercial training-free baselines receive 0% preference, only 34 cases are used, and the pairwise aggregation/confidence intervals are not sufficiently explained.
The real-image evaluation is limited and depends on inversion quality; the paper itself admits this limitation, but the main claims are much broader than the demonstrated evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are scattered, no clear algorithmic pseudocode is provided, and the paper refers to a website without giving concrete reproducibility artifacts in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: precise text-guided color editing while preserving geometry, material appearance, illumination, reflections, and non-edited regions. The motivation is clear and well connected to the shift from U-Net diffusion models to MM-DiT architectures.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and well matched to the architecture: using vision-to-vision attention for structure preservation, vision-to-text attention for mask extraction, vision value-token copying for non-edit-region color preservation, and text-to-vision attention for attribute re-weighting is a coherent decomposition.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The authors compare against multiple training-free baselines, commercial systems, two image backbones, a video backbone, real-image editing settings, and instruction-based editing models. This breadth makes the contribution more convincing than a narrow benchmark-only result.

Quantitative results are consistently favorable across PIE-Bench and the larger ColorCtrl-Bench, with strong gains in structure/background preservation metrics and additional GPT-4o-based SC/PQ metrics that better expose color-edit success than CLIP alone.

The qualitative examples are compelling, especially for preserving texture, semi-transparency, reflections, shadows, and temporal coherence in video. The ablations support the usefulness of the structure preservation and color preservation components.
The paper includes useful implementation details, baseline adaptation details, limitations, ethics, and an LLM-usage statement. The method appears relatively easy to reproduce if code is released.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is an effective combination of attention swapping, mask extraction, value-token copying, and attention re-weighting adapted to MM-DiT, but it does not introduce a fundamentally new learning or inference principle. Its conceptual distance from prior attention-control methods could be positioned more sharply.

The main benchmark setting is largely noise-to-image rather than true real-image editing. This isolates editing behavior, but it also avoids the difficult inversion/reconstruction issues that dominate practical image editing. Real-image results are included, but they are less central and comparatively limited.

Several claims about physical consistency, material preservation, and light-matter interactions are stronger than the evidence. The paper mostly evaluates image similarity and visual plausibility rather than physically grounded properties such as consistent reflectance, illumination spectra, or explicit shadow/reflection correctness.

The evaluation relies heavily on automatic metrics with known limitations. CLIP is acknowledged as problematic, while SC/PQ are produced by GPT-4o, which introduces dependence on a proprietary judge and possible evaluation instability. Human evaluation is helpful but small, and the reported zero preferences for many baselines raises questions about task design or comparison aggregation.

ColorCtrl-Bench is generated by GPT prompts, and the benchmark construction may not fully cover difficult real-world ambiguity, multi-object binding, occlusion, fine-grained material variation, or adversarial prompt cases. More dataset validation would strengthen confidence.

The commercial-model comparison is interesting but not entirely apples-to-apples: commercial systems may optimize different editing objectives, and the paper’s own method uses generated sources and internal attention access. The conclusion that the method surpasses commercial models should be qualified more carefully.

Reproducibility is not complete at submission time because the authors only commit to releasing code upon acceptance. Given the number of baseline reimplementations and tuned hyperparameters, code and generated benchmark assets are important for verifying the results.

The limitation analysis is honest but short. Failure modes involving incorrect localization, ambiguous noun binding, multiple instances of the same object, real-image inversion quality, and non-color edits deserve more systematic evaluation.
